title: Filtering with WHERE
summary: WHERE filters rows by a rule. Only rows that match the rule appear in the answer.
introduction: WHERE filters rows by a rule. Only rows that match the rule appear in the answer. Ask for books above a page count or items with a certain name. Try a rule that matches several rows and one that matches none.
learningObjectives: Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT
Compare text and ISO dates correctly

blocks.text: `WHERE` comes after `FROM` and holds a condition. The database evaluates it for every row and keeps the rows where it is true. The condition can use any column of the table, even one you do not select.

blocks.code: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > 10;

blocks.content:
name                | price
--------------------+------
USB cable           | 12
Mechanical keyboard | 89
Monitor stand       | 39.5

blocks.text: `<>` is the standard not-equal operator; `!=` is accepted by every major database as well. Text values go in single quotes; numbers do not. Writing `price > '10'` happens to work (SQLite converts the text, and PostgreSQL treats a quoted literal as untyped), but mixing types is a habit that breaks as soon as a real text column is involved, so keep the types matching: quotes around text and dates, none around numbers.

A condition is evaluated for one row at a time, so it can only compare values of that row with constants or with each other; it cannot ask about other rows ("customers who ordered more than Ada"). Questions like that need a join or a subquery, which come later in the tutorial.

blocks.code: SELECT name, country FROM customers WHERE country <> 'US';

blocks.content:
name             | country
-----------------+------------
Ada Lovelace     | UK
Linus Torvalds   | Finland
Guido van Rossum | Netherlands

blocks.text: `AND` requires both conditions to be true, `OR` requires at least one, and `NOT` inverts a condition. Office products under 20:

blocks.content:
name      | category | price
----------+----------+------
Mouse pad | Office   | 8.99

blocks.text: `OR` keeps a row when either side is true: `WHERE country = 'UK' OR country = 'Finland'` lists Ada and Linus. `NOT` flips a condition, so `WHERE NOT country = 'US'` means the same as `country <> 'US'`; it becomes more useful with the operators of the next lesson, where `NOT LIKE`, `NOT IN` and `NOT BETWEEN` read almost like English. Conditions can be chained as far as you like, which is exactly where the next trap lies.

When a condition mixes AND and OR, `AND` is evaluated first, like multiplication before addition. The query below *looks* like it asks for cheap office and stationery items, but it actually returns all office products plus the stationery under 3:

blocks.content:
name          | category   | price
--------------+------------+------
Mouse pad     | Office     | 8.99
Monitor stand | Office     | 39.5
Sticky notes  | Stationery | 2.75

blocks.text: Parentheses make the intended grouping explicit and change the result:

blocks.content:
name         | category   | price
-------------+------------+------
Sticky notes | Stationery | 2.75

blocks.title: Mixing AND and OR without parentheses
blocks.text: This is the most common WHERE bug, and it never produces an error message, only wrong rows. Whenever a condition contains both `AND` and `OR`, add parentheses even when they are not strictly needed; the next person reading the query will thank you.

Text comparisons are case-sensitive in SQLite and PostgreSQL (`'US'` and `'us'` are different values), while MySQL's default collations ignore case. Dates in this database are stored as ISO 8601 text (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a format whose alphabetical order is also chronological order, so `>=` works on them as expected:

blocks.code: SELECT name, joined FROM customers WHERE joined >= '2025-01-01';

blocks.content:
name              | joined
------------------+-----------
Margaret Hamilton | 2025-02-09
Guido van Rossum  | 2025-05-30

blocks.text: A query whose condition matches nothing is not an error. The playground prints `OK` and no table, as this lower-case search shows:

blocks.code: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country = 'us';

blocks.content: OK: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country = 'us'

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Find the products that cost between 5 and 50 using two comparisons joined by `AND`, then wrap the whole condition in `NOT (...)` to get the other products.

blocks.title: Try it yourself

questions.question: Which rows does `WHERE price > 10 AND category = 'Office'` return?
questions.explanation: AND requires both conditions to hold for the same row: the product must be in the Office category and cost more than 10.
options: Products that are either over 10 or in Office

questions.question: Text values in a WHERE condition are enclosed in ___ quotes.
questions.explanation: Single quotes mark text values in SQL. Double quotes are reserved for identifiers such as column names.

seo.title: SQL WHERE – Filter Rows with AND, OR and NOT
seo.description: Learn the SQL WHERE clause: comparison operators, combining conditions with AND, OR and NOT, precedence and parentheses, and text and date comparisons.
